about.access.p: A learner who is blind or has low vision gets a braille mode — six-key entry, a curriculum in cells, spoken guidance — rather than the sighted page read aloud. Everyone else gets an accessibility page with five settings that combine freely, and every individual switch underneath: hold animations still, a typeface for dyslexia, larger things to press, never two keys at once, ignore a key that repeats itself, say mistakes in sound, write down what is spoken. Set per learner, because a household shares one login and the person who needs them is not always the one who set the account up.
about.access.p2: Names describe what each one does, never a condition. Nobody should have to identify themselves with a diagnosis to make an app usable.
about.family.p: One account holds a profile for each person in your home, and every profile keeps its own progress. Kids step into a friendly dino-run adventure that scales to their age — shorter sessions, gentler pacing, and bigger encouragement for the youngest — while grown-ups get the full practice screen with detailed statistics. Everyone learns on the same proven engine, just dressed for their age.
about.foot: keylearn · v{version} · learn to type, joyfully
about.glance.1: KeyLearn is a free, open-source touch-typing tutor for the whole household — grown-ups and kids alike.
about.glance.2: It watches the keys that slow you down and builds your practice around them, so every minute is spent where it counts.
about.glance.3: Children get a playful dino-run world that adapts to their age; grown-ups get a focused, data-rich practice screen; and a learner who is blind gets a braille mode built for the purpose.
about.glance.4: No ads, no trackers, and your data stays yours.
about.glance.label: In a sentence
about.how.p: Rather than marching you through fixed drills, KeyLearn measures how quickly and cleanly you hit each key and weaves your weak spots into the words it generates. A letter only joins your set once you can type it both quickly and accurately, so the difficulty rises exactly as fast as you do — never faster.
about.inside.p1: Two courses, because people differ: Guided practice adapts to the keys that slow you down, and Classic course is the fixed ladder a typing book would give you. There is a third for code — real snippets in the language you choose, so brackets and indentation get the drilling prose never gives them.
about.inside.p2: Alongside them: a speed test, keyboard layouts to compare, high scores, and races against other people in real time. Finish a course and there is a certificate with a number anybody can check — issued by us, honest about what it is, and not pretending to be a qualification somebody else recognises.
about.maker.p: KeyLearn is designed and built by AK, an independent developer working mostly solo. It started at the kitchen table, watching a young family member hunt-and-peck at a keyboard and wishing for something that felt more like a game than a chore. AK has spent years building software for the web, but this is the first project made squarely for family — no company behind it, no investors to please, just care put into a tool meant to be genuinely useful. Feedback and contributions are always welcome.
about.oss.p: KeyLearn is published under the GNU AGPL license: the whole source code is open for you to read, run, or improve. Learning to type is free — every lesson, every learner in your household, and no advertising. If you find it useful you can support the project, but nothing here is held back until you do. Your practice data belongs to you: export it or erase it whenever you like. View the source on GitHub.
about.support.p: KeyLearn is free for every learner, and that’s never going to change. If it’s helped you or your kids, buying a coffee helps keep it going. Buy me a coffee.
about.title: About KeyLearn
about.values.1: Learners first. Every decision is judged by one question — does it help someone type better and enjoy getting there?
about.values.2: Kindness over pressure. Progress is celebrated, mistakes are forgiven, and no one is shamed into practising.
about.values.3: Privacy by default. No ads, no trackers, no selling data. Practise as a guest and nothing ever leaves your device.
about.values.4: Open and honest. The whole source is public, the language is plain, and there are no dark patterns or hidden costs.
about.values.5: Built to last. Careful, unhurried work over hype — a tool you can trust for years, not a growth experiment.
about.version.p: You’re running KeyLearn v{version}. Each release bumps this number so you always know which build you’re on. See what changed.
about.why.p: Typing well is a quiet superpower, and KeyLearn teaches it the encouraging way — short sessions, honest feedback, and steady progress you can feel. It began in 2026, built on keybr, an open-source typing tutor that had already figured out the hard part: adapting to the keys that slow you down. From there it grew into a typing tutor for the whole family — a playful dino-run world for kids, per-learner household profiles, age-aware pacing, and support for many languages.
accessibility.five.1: Calm. Nothing moves, nothing counts, nothing is timed. A missed day does not break the run.
accessibility.five.2: Fewer things at once. Practice opens with the words and the keyboard, and nothing else asking to be looked at.
accessibility.five.3: Easier to read. The typeface built for dyslexia, more space between the letters and the lines, and stronger text against the page.
accessibility.five.4: Colours apart. Finger colours that stay distinct under colour blindness, and mistakes said in sound as well as in red.
accessibility.five.5: Steadier hands. Bigger things to press, no two keys at once, and a key that repeats itself is not counted twice.
accessibility.five.p1: Account → Accessibility. Turn on as many as you need — they combine, because the needs do. Somebody dyslexic with a tremor needs two of them, and being made to choose one would be the app asking which disability to accommodate.
accessibility.five.p2: They are named for what they do, never for a condition. Nobody should have to identify themselves with a diagnosis to make an app usable.
accessibility.five.p3: Under them, a section you can open with every switch on its own — fifteen of them — for anyone who wants to disagree with a setting rather than accept it whole. And one button that puts every one of them back.
accessibility.glance.1: There is an Accessibility page in your account with five settings you can turn on in any combination, and every individual switch underneath them. It is set per learner, so one person’s adjustments do not change anybody else’s.
accessibility.glance.2: A learner who is blind or has low vision can practise here — there is a braille mode with six-key entry and spoken guidance, not a bolted-on screen-reader afterthought.
accessibility.glance.3: Everything is reachable from the keyboard, which is the one input device a typing tutor can be sure of.
accessibility.glance.4: We aim at WCAG 2.2 Level AA. We have not been independently audited, so we tell you what we know rather than claiming a grade.
accessibility.glance.5: Something in your way? Write to <supportLink>support@keylearn.org</supportLink> and a person will read it.
accessibility.glance.5b: Something in your way? <supportLink>Tell us</supportLink> and a person will read it.
accessibility.short.1: The standard practice page is not narrated. The text being typed is not announced to a screen reader, because announcing every keystroke would make it unusable. A learner who needs speech should use the braille mode, which is built for exactly this and is switched on per learner in the account settings.
accessibility.short.2: We have had no independent audit. Everything on this page is our own assessment of our own work, which is the weakest kind of evidence there is.
accessibility.short.3: The kids worlds are visual. The dinosaur and hero scenes carry encouragement rather than instruction, so nothing is lost by not seeing them — but they are not described, and a child who cannot see them is getting a plainer experience than one who can.
accessibility.short.4: The settings are per learner, and per device. They are kept with the learner’s profile on the device you set them on. Sign in on a new machine and you will need to set them again — which is exactly the wrong way round, because the person most inconvenienced by re-doing them is the person who needs them.
accessibility.short.5: Nothing here has been tested with real assistive technology by the people who use it. The braille mode was built with the standard in front of us, not a braille reader beside us. If you use one, we would rather hear that we got it wrong than not hear at all.
accessibility.short.p: We would rather say this plainly than have you discover it.
accessibility.switches.bounce: A key that repeats itself. A tremor or a sticky switch sends the same letter twice. This ignores a repeat that arrives within a window you set, up to a fifth of a second — never more, because past that a deliberate double letter starts being eaten, and a filter that loses real keystrokes is worse than none.
accessibility.switches.braille: Braille and audio. A learner set up with vision support gets a different page altogether: six-key braille entry, a curriculum in cells rather than letters, and spoken guidance throughout. It is a separate way of learning to type, not the sighted page read aloud.
accessibility.switches.calm: Celebrations that hold still. The kids world shakes after a wrong key and throws sparks when something goes right. Neither is a flashing hazard — nothing in the app crosses three flashes a second, and we measured — but a hard shake arrives exactly when a child is already struggling. The colour stays, because it carries the meaning; the movement goes.
accessibility.switches.captions: What is said aloud, written down. The braille page and the kids coach both speak. For a learner who is deaf or hard of hearing, speech that is not written is an instruction they were never given. Speech rate and voice are yours to set as well.
accessibility.switches.chords: Never two keys at once. Capitals need a shift held down while another key is pressed. For a one-handed learner or anyone who cannot hold two keys, this takes capitals and punctuation out of the lessons rather than making them a barrier to the alphabet.
accessibility.switches.contrast: Colour you choose, checked. Households can mix their own colours, and the app measures the contrast of what you pick against the page and refuses combinations nobody could read. Turning on a setting that asks for clearer text lifts the quiet parts of the interface too — the rules, chart frames and keyboard outlines go to 3:1 against the page, which is what WCAG asks of anything that is not text.
accessibility.switches.cues: Mistakes you can hear. A wrong keystroke is red, and red is exactly what a learner with a colour vision difference may not see. This turns on the error tone so the same fact arrives by ear.
accessibility.switches.keyboardFirst: Keyboard first. Every control can be operated from the keyboard, and a skip link at the top of each page takes you straight to the lesson without walking the header and the menus.
accessibility.switches.motion: Motion, twice over. If your device asks for reduced motion the app listens — including the scenes drawn on canvas that a stylesheet alone would not reach. There is also a switch here, because the system setting is all-or-nothing across every app on the machine and somebody may want films to move and this page to hold still.
accessibility.switches.predictable: Always the same words. The coach picks its lines at random so encouragement does not turn into wallpaper. For an autistic learner that same property reads differently: a surprise where reassurance should be is not a delight. This makes the app say the same thing in the same place every time.
accessibility.switches.safeZones: A keyboard for colour blindness. The finger colours are what the keyboard teaches with, and the usual set does not survive red-green colour blindness — measured, its two closest neighbouring zones are at the threshold of being the same colour for a protanope. There is an alternative set chosen to stay apart under both common forms, and separately a finger number on every key, so the zones can be read without depending on colour at all. That is the stronger of the two: colour must never be the only way of conveying anything.
accessibility.switches.targets: Larger things to press. WCAG 2.2 asks for 24×24 pixels at AA and 44×44 at AAA. The app meets the first everywhere; this setting asks for the second, which is what a learner with a tremor or a touchscreen actually needs.
accessibility.switches.textSize: Text you can see. The practice text scales independently of the rest of the page, so it can be made large without breaking the layout around it.
accessibility.switches.timers: Time you control. Nothing is scored against a countdown you cannot change; session length is a setting, and a lesson interrupted is simply restarted rather than failed. The running figures and the clock can both be hidden outright, and a missed day can be set not to break a streak — a streak that punishes illness is a streak that punishes disability.
accessibility.switches.typeface: A typeface for dyslexia. OpenDyslexic, with weighted bottoms so b, d, p and q cannot rotate into one another. Alongside it, letter spacing and line height you can set yourself — spacing is the reading support with the best evidence behind it, ahead of the typeface, and on a page somebody reads one letter at a time it is worth more here than anywhere else.
accessibility.telling.ai: An assistant reads it first and answers what it can. It always says it is an AI, never pretends otherwise, and a person takes over the moment you ask for one — you will not have to ask twice.
accessibility.telling.p1: If something here blocks you or a learner you are responsible for, write to <supportLink>support@keylearn.org</supportLink>. Say what you were trying to do and what happened; you do not need to know the name of the standard it breaks. We will reply, and if it is our fault we will say so and tell you when it is fixed.
accessibility.telling.p1b: If something here blocks you or a learner you are responsible for, <supportLink>tell us</supportLink>. Say what you were trying to do and what happened; you do not need to know the name of the standard it breaks. We will reply, and if it is our fault we will say so and tell you when it is fixed.
accessibility.telling.p2: For schools and public bodies: we are happy to answer a procurement questionnaire against WCAG 2.2 or EN 301 549, on the understanding that our answers are self-assessed and this page is the honest version of them.
account.a11y.bounce: Ignore a key that repeats itself
account.a11y.bounce.sub: A hand that shakes sends one press twice. The second is dropped rather than counted as a mistake — the window is far shorter than a deliberate double letter.
account.a11y.calm.sub: The kids world shakes after a wrong key and throws sparks when something goes right. The colours stay; the movement goes.
account.a11y.captions: Write down what is said aloud
account.a11y.captions.sub: The braille page and the kids coach both speak. This puts every line on screen as it is said, for a learner who cannot hear it — or a grown-up sitting beside one.
account.a11y.chords.sub: Capitals and most punctuation need Shift and a letter together. Off, the lessons ask only for what one finger at a time can reach.
account.a11y.contrast.sub: How hard the words work to be read. Each step is a measured level rather than a matter of taste — the theme keeps its colours, the text is lifted away from them.
account.a11y.cues.sub: A wrong key is shown in red, and red is the thing some eyes cannot pick out. This says the same in a tone, so nothing depends on colour alone.
account.a11y.fingerMarks: A finger number on every key
account.a11y.fingerMarks.sub: The zones say which finger with colour. This says it in a character as well, so nothing depends on telling the colours apart.
account.a11y.motion.sub: Your device's own setting is already followed. This one is for wanting the rest of the machine to move and this page not to.
account.a11y.plain.sub: Practice opens with the words and the keyboard. The figures, the trend and the journey strip stay away until you ask for them back.
account.a11y.predictable.sub: The coach picks its encouragement at random so it does not become wallpaper. This makes it say the same line every time, for a learner who is listening for what the app will say.
account.a11y.preset.calm.sub: Nothing moves, nothing counts, nothing is timed. A missed day does not break the run.
account.a11y.preset.colour.sub: Finger colours that stay distinct, and mistakes said in sound as well as in red.
account.a11y.preset.focus.sub: Practice opens with the words and the keyboard, and nothing else asking to be looked at.
account.a11y.preset.hands.sub: Bigger things to press, no two keys at once, and a shake is not read as a mistake.
account.a11y.preset.read.sub: Stronger text against the page, and letters that cannot be mistaken for one another.
account.a11y.presets: Turn on as many of these as you need
account.a11y.reset.sub: Every one of these is off until somebody asks for it. This puts them all back.
account.a11y.scores.sub: The speed, the accuracy and the score come off the screen while you type. Nothing stops being recorded — they are shown afterwards, when they are information rather than a race.
account.a11y.spacing.sub: Spacing helps a struggling reader more than any typeface does. This applies to the practice text — the words being read one letter at a time.
account.a11y.speechRate.sub: Somebody who listens all day listens fast. This is the same speed the braille page uses for every word it speaks.
account.a11y.speechVoice.sub: Your device's voices. Left alone, the app uses whichever one matches the language of the page.
account.a11y.streak: A rest day keeps the streak
account.a11y.streak.sub: A missed day is forgiven rather than counted, so the number stays a true count of days practised. Nobody should have to choose between resting and starting again.
account.a11y.targets.sub: Buttons and links grow to the size a hand that is not quite steady can reach without aiming.
account.a11y.timers.sub: Hides every countdown and running time. The practice is exactly the same; what goes is being watched while you do it.
account.a11y.tuning.sub: Every switch a preset touches, and a few it does not.
account.a11y.typeface.sub: Letters with weighted bottoms and shapes that cannot be mistaken for one another when they rotate — b for d, p for q.

help.adaptive.bigrams:
Drilling the letter pairs that trip you up

Not everything that slows you down is a single key. Often it’s the hand-off between two — an awkward pair like ‘ny’, ‘rl’ or ‘br’ where your fingers have to travel or cross over. KeyLearn keeps an eye on the pairings where you consistently stumble and weaves more of them into the words it builds for you, so you smooth out the transitions themselves, not just the individual letters on either side.
help.adaptive.confidence:
Confidence that watches accuracy, not just speed

The core signal for how well you know a key has always been how fast you type it. KeyLearn now adds a second opinion drawn from learning science — a technique called Bayesian Knowledge Tracing — that also weighs how cleanly you hit that key. It forgives the occasional slip on a key you clearly know, and it refuses to be fooled by a lucky fast-but-sloppy tap. The two views are blended together, with raw speed still leading by two-to-one, so a letter only counts as mastered when you’re both quick and accurate. It’s tuned to unlock the next letter at the same comfortable pace you’re used to — usually a couple of clean passes — just with a sharper eye on mistakes.
help.adaptive.decay:
Letters quietly fade if you leave them alone

Skills rust when they go unused, and KeyLearn reflects that honestly. A key you haven’t practiced in a long time slowly loses a little confidence over real time, so you might see an old letter drift back from green toward red on its own. That’s not you getting worse — it’s the app gently flagging that the letter is due for a refresh before it truly slips. Your best-ever result for a key is never wiped out; only the current reading softens.
help.adaptive.intro:
The smart layers working behind the scenes

The letter-by-letter cycle above is the backbone of your practice, but KeyLearn runs a few extra adaptive helpers on top of it. You never switch these on or think about them — they quietly shape every session so your time lands where it pays off most. Here’s what each one is doing while you type.
help.adaptive.review:
A quick warm-up on the keys you’re due to review

Letters you picked up a while ago but haven’t touched in a few sessions get surfaced first, as a short warm-up at the start of your practice. It works the way a good flashcard deck resurfaces a card right before you’d forget it: reviewing a skill at that fading edge is exactly what pushes it into long-term memory. So don’t be surprised to revisit an old friend before meeting anyone new.
help.example1: Example 1 went from 30 to 70 WPM over 15 days, with 4 hours 20 minutes of total practice — the accuracy-aware confidence blend kept steering each session toward the keys that were genuinely holding them back.
help.example2: Example 2 climbed from 35 to 70 WPM over 12 days, with just 2 hours and 20 minutes of practice — the spaced-review warm-up meant less time was needed to make each gain stick.
help.example3: Example 3 made a solid leap from under 20 to 40 WPM over 11 days, with 5 hours and 30 minutes of practice — the bigram drills smoothing out the awkward letter pairs that had been the real bottleneck.
help.example4: Example 4 held steady at roughly 70 WPM (already quite fast) across 11 days and 2 hours 10 minutes of practice, while accuracy kept climbing — the BKT blend only marks a key mastered once it’s both fast and clean, so the extra reps went straight into fewer mistakes.
help.example5: Example 5 improved from 20 to 45 WPM over 22 days and about 10 hours of practice (progress isn’t always fast, and that’s okay) — and whenever older letters faded, the decay nudges surfaced them again for a quick refresh before they slipped for real.

help.rule1.body: The very first time you practice, KeyLearn has no data on your skills yet, so it sticks to a handful of the most frequent letters — things like ‘E’, ‘N’, ‘I’, ‘A’, ‘R’ and ‘L’ — to build your first words. Every word you see will be made only from this starter set; the rest of the alphabet stays out of play for now. Since there’s no typing data yet for these letters, their indicators show up gray.
help.rule1.title: It starts with a handful of letters
help.rule2.body: Once you start typing the generated words, KeyLearn starts logging your performance, and you’ll see the indicators shift from red toward green. Red marks a key you’re typing slowly, while green marks one you’re typing quickly. Your job at this stage is to turn every letter green by picking up speed. Notice that in this example, ‘A’ is called out because it has the slowest typing speed of the bunch, which makes it the target letter. That target letter shows up in every word you’re given — worth remembering, because it means you’re always drilling the exact key that’s currently slowing you down.
help.rule2.title: You get comfortable with those letters
help.rule3.body: Once your speed picks up and every letter has turned green, a new letter — ‘T’ — joins the set, and the words you’re given from now on are drawn from this larger pool. ‘T’ becomes the new target letter and appears in every word. As before, since there’s no data on it yet, its indicator starts out gray.
help.rule3.title: More letters join the set
help.rule4.body: Now your goal is to turn this newest letter green too, and once you do, another letter gets added and the whole cycle repeats. In practice, don’t be surprised if the letters you’d already mastered slip back toward red for a while, as shown here — that’s completely normal. Your focus doesn’t change: get the current target letter to green so the next one unlocks.
help.rule4.title: You master the newly added letters
help.rule5.body: Stick with it, and eventually every single letter will turn green. That’s the main milestone, and you should feel great about reaching it! It doesn’t have to be the end, though — keep practicing for as long as you’d like.
help.rule5.title: Rinse and repeat
help.section1:
Type faster, the smart way

What is touch typing?

KeyLearn teaches you touch typing — hitting the right keys from muscle memory alone, with no need to glance down at the keyboard. Mastering it can dramatically boost both your speed and accuracy. Its opposite is hunt-and-peck typing, where you keep your eyes on the keys instead of the screen and rely on just your index fingers.
help.section2:
How the lessons are built

KeyLearn takes a different approach: it leans on statistics and adaptive algorithms to build typing drills tailored to exactly where your skills stand right now. It does this by looping through three steps:

  1. Based on the typing data gathered so far, the algorithm figures out your current skill level and generates a batch of random words built from a letter set it chooses for you.
  2. You type those words, aiming to keep your mistakes to a minimum.
  3. While you type, the algorithm records fresh statistics — including how long each key takes you to hit — and feeds them back into step one to build the next batch of words.

All you have to do at every stage is type the words you’re given; KeyLearn handles the rest.
help.section3:
How words are generated

KeyLearn builds random words that still sound natural and readable, following the phonetic patterns of your native language — many of them could pass for real words, and some are. Typing text that reads sensibly is far easier than typing a jumble of random letters, and it also helps you internalize the key combinations you’ll hit most often. That second part matters a lot: in English, for instance, the letter ‘W’ almost never follows ‘Z’, so this app will never ask you to type that pairing. Instead, you’ll practice far more common sequences like ‘the’, ‘that’, and ‘with’ — before long, you’ll be flying through the ‘th’ combo.

Proper keyboard hand placement

Rest all your fingers on the home row — the row that contains the Caps Lock key. You’ll feel small raised bumps on the ‘F’ and ‘J’ keys; line your index fingers up with those. From there, every finger owns a specific group of keys, shown in the illustration below.

m_tour01:
Type Faster With Confidence

KeyLearn teaches you touch typing — typing from muscle memory instead of hunting for keys with your eyes. It can boost both your speed and accuracy by a wide margin. The alternative is hunt-and-peck typing, where you keep glancing down at the keyboard and rely mostly on your index fingers.

This short walkthrough covers how the app works.

Use the left and right arrow keys to move between these slides.
m_tour02:
Here’s what our teaching approach is built on:

No tedious drilling. Unlike many typing tutors, KeyLearn never makes you repeat the same block like ‘jjf jjk jjf jjk’ over and over. That gets tiresome fast and barely helps you learn.

Instead, an algorithm builds lessons that match your current skill level. Each lesson is made of random words drawn from a subset of your alphabet’s letters. The algorithm decides how large that subset is and how often each letter shows up, aiming to give you the most effective learning experience.
m_tour03:
At the start, words are generated from just a handful of the alphabet’s most common letters.

As you type those words, the app tracks a time-to-type measurement for each letter in the subset. That measurement is how your progress gets tracked — the more comfortable you get with a letter, the faster you type it.

Once you’re comfortable with the whole current subset, the algorithm grows it by folding in additional letters.
m_tour04:
Whenever a new letter joins the subset, its frequency gets boosted so it shows up in nearly every generated word of a lesson.

The algorithm also reshuffles letter frequencies on purpose, giving more weight to whichever letters have the slowest time-to-type readings.

In practice, that keeps you typing the letters you’re least comfortable with.
m_tour05: This is the text board, showing the passage you need to type. It refreshes with every new lesson and is built automatically from your current letter subset. Most of these words aren’t real — they’re generated from your language’s phonetic rules so they still sound natural and are easy to pronounce. It’s a bit playful, and it also lets us draw from a far larger pool of words than actually exist.
m_tour06: This is the virtual keyboard, which helps you memorize where each key sits. Use it to locate keys instead of glancing down at your physical keyboard. Your keyboard’s F and J keys have small raised bumps — feel for these to line up your index fingers without looking. Once your index fingers are correctly placed, you’ll be able to find every other key from there.
m_tour07:
This shows your typing speed and how it compares to your average. Higher numbers here are the goal.

Speed is measured in either Words per Minute (WPM) or Characters per Minute (CPM). Since a word is standardized to five characters, 10WPM works out to 50CPM.

You can toggle between WPM and CPM on the Settings page.
m_tour08:
This is your accuracy reading, along with how it compares to your average. As with speed, higher is better here.

Accuracy is the percentage of characters you typed correctly. Repeated mistakes at the same spot only count as a single error.
m_tour09:
This is your score, shown in abstract points, along with how it differs from your average.

It’s calculated from your speed, your error count, and how many letters are currently in your set. The formula rewards fast typing and penalizes mistakes, so typing quickly while making lots of errors won’t earn you a high score.
m_tour10: This trail maps the letters currently used to build your lessons, in the order you unlock them, each one coloured by how confident you are with it:
m_tour11: Hovering a stop on the trail forecasts how many lessons remain before that letter fully unlocks, as shown in the sample chart below. Check back often for a clearer picture of how your learning is progressing.
m_tour12:
This shows details for the letter that’s currently boosted in frequency and appearing in every generated word:

Top typing speed
The fastest you’ve ever typed this particular letter.
Confidence score
A value between zero and one, calculated from your typing speed, showing how well you know this letter. Once confidence reaches one, the letter counts as fully learned.
Learning rate
How your speed on this letter is trending from lesson to lesson.

privacy.changes.p: Any change to this policy appears on this page with an updated date at the top. We’ll keep it in plain language — if you ever find a sentence here that needs a lawyer to decode, that’s a bug.
privacy.children.p1: A child does not have an account here. They have a profile inside an adult’s account, and everything about that profile is the account holder’s to see, change and delete. Children can also practise fully in guest mode, where no personal information is asked for or sent anywhere at all.
privacy.children.p2: Accounts are for adults. Creating one asks for a date of birth and we do not knowingly accept one from a child; where a sign-in provider is used, their own age rules apply on top. Adding a child’s profile asks the account holder to confirm they are the parent or guardian, and the confirmation is recorded with the date.
privacy.children.p3: A child’s profile is kept to the minimum that makes the app work: a first name — a nickname is fine — an optional birth year, and their practice. We do not ask for a school, an address, a photograph or a contact detail for a child, and there is no way for one child to contact another.
privacy.children.p4: An account can be locked behind a parent PIN, so a child using the family device cannot change account settings, delete profiles or reach anything meant for the adult.
privacy.children.p5: If you believe a child has created an account here without a parent’s involvement, write to <supportLink>support@keylearn.org</supportLink> and we will delete it.
privacy.children.p5b: If you believe a child has created an account here without a parent’s involvement, tell us through <supportLink>our support page</supportLink> and we will delete it.
privacy.collect.certificates: Certificates — a certificate records the name printed on it, the language, the level, the speed and the accuracy achieved, and a number. Anybody given the number can check it on our Check a certificate page — that is the point of it. Whether the name is shown to the person checking is a choice you make when it is issued; if you keep it hidden, the page confirms the certificate is real without naming the holder.
privacy.collect.emailCode: A link or code by e-mail — a short-lived code is stored until it is used or expires, then deleted.
privacy.collect.guest: As a guest — nothing reaches us. Your lesson results, learner profiles, settings and streaks are stored in your own browser, in local storage and in a database the browser keeps on your device. They stay there; we cannot see them, and clearing your browser data removes them.
privacy.collect.learners: Learners in your household — a profile carries a first name, an optional last name, an optional birth year, an avatar and that learner’s own settings. Signed out, profiles never leave the device. Signed in, they are stored so a household can practise on more than one machine. A birth year is used to choose the right certificate and nothing else; you can leave it out.
privacy.collect.logs: Like every website — our servers briefly keep routine technical logs (IP address, browser type, request time) to keep the service secure and diagnose problems. These logs rotate away automatically and are not used to profile you.
privacy.collect.mail: E-mail we send you — verification codes, sign-in links and security alerts go out through an e-mail delivery provider, which necessarily handles your address to deliver them. We do not send marketing.
privacy.collect.passkey: A passkey — a public key and a counter. The private half never leaves your device and cannot be extracted from what we hold.
privacy.collect.password: A password — kept only as a one-way hash. We cannot read it, and neither can anybody who takes a copy of our database.
privacy.collect.payment: If you support the project — payment is handled by our payment provider. We receive a record that a payment happened; we never see or store your card details.
privacy.collect.provider: A sign-in provider such as Google — we keep the identifier they give us and the basics they share: a name, an avatar, a link. We never see your password with them.
privacy.collect.security: Security events — sign-ins, failed sign-ins, password changes, a passkey added or removed, and similar. Each is kept with the IP address and browser it came from, so that you can see it on your own account page and recognise something you did not do. This is the one place we deliberately keep an IP address against your account.
privacy.collect.signinIntro: If you sign in — we store an e-mail address, a display name, and your typing statistics, so they can follow you across devices. How you prove it is you is up to you, and each choice stores something different:
privacy.collect.support: Messages you send support — what you write to us, any files you attach, the country our network sees the request coming from and the time zone your browser reports. An assistant reads it first to answer what it can, which means the text of your message is processed by the AI provider that runs it; it always identifies itself as an AI, and a person takes over whenever that is the better answer. Conversations stay on your account so you can come back to them, and you can remove any of them from your list at any time.
privacy.collect.twostep: Two-step verification — a shared secret for your authenticator app, and your unused recovery codes.
privacy.cookies.p: KeyLearn uses only what’s strictly necessary: a session cookie that keeps you signed in, and local preference storage for things like your theme and settings. There are no marketing or tracking cookies — which is why you don’t see a cookie banner here.
privacy.glance.1: Practice as a guest and your data never leaves your browser.
privacy.glance.2: Sign in and we store your e-mail, a name, your learner profiles and your typing statistics — and nothing else about you.
privacy.glance.3: No ads, no third-party trackers, no analytics scripts, and we never sell your data — to anyone, for any reason.
privacy.glance.4: You can export or permanently delete everything, any time, in a couple of clicks.
privacy.never.1: We don’t sell, rent, or trade your personal data.
privacy.never.2: We don’t show ads or embed advertising networks.
privacy.never.3: We don’t run third-party trackers or marketing analytics on your practice.
privacy.never.4: We don’t read more from your sign-in provider than the basics needed to log you in.
privacy.rights.ask: Ask — anything about your data, or about KeyLearn itself, reaches a person at support@keylearn.org.
privacy.rights.ask2: Ask — anything about your data, or about KeyLearn itself, reaches a person through our support page.
privacy.rights.complain: Complain — if you believe we’ve mishandled your data, write to us first at support@keylearn.org, and you can contact your local data-protection authority at any time.
privacy.rights.complain2: Complain — if you believe we’ve mishandled your data, tell us first through our support page, and you can contact your local data-protection authority at any time.
privacy.rights.correct: Correct it — your name, e-mail and every learner profile can be edited in your account. If your name and avatar came from a sign-in provider, changing them there updates them here too.
privacy.rights.erase: Erase it — “clear statistics” wipes your typing history, and deleting your account permanently removes everything from our servers. Both are irreversible, and that’s the point.
privacy.rights.p: Wherever you live — under the EU and UK GDPR, California’s CCPA/CPRA, and similar laws around the world — the same rights apply to every KeyLearn user, built straight into the app:
privacy.rights.see: See and take your data — the export button on your profile downloads everything we have as a portable file.
privacy.rights.takeOut: Take one learner out — deleting a learner profile removes that learner’s practice history without touching anybody else’s in the household.
privacy.security.p1: All traffic is encrypted in transit. Passwords are stored only as one-way hashes, and a passkey’s private half never reaches us at all. We keep your data only for as long as you keep your account — delete it and the data goes too. Security events age out on their own, and unused e-mail codes are deleted as soon as they expire.
privacy.security.p2: Deleting your account erases your name and e-mail from our servers. Two things deliberately survive it: a certificate you have already been issued stays checkable, because a qualification that silently stops verifying is worth nothing to the person holding it — and anything we are required to keep for accounting where you have paid us. You can ask us to withdraw a certificate.
privacy.security.p3: No system is perfectly secure, so we keep what we store to a minimum; if a breach ever affects your data, we will notify you as the law requires.

profile.road.childPace.building.1: {speed} today, and every session builds on it. What matters at this age is turning up regularly and using the right fingers; speed follows on its own, over years, and pushing for it now mostly teaches habits that are hard to undo.
profile.road.childPace.building.2: {speed} at the moment, and slow is completely normal here. What is being built is the map of which finger goes where — and once that is automatic, pace arrives without anyone chasing it.
profile.road.childPace.building.3: {speed} so far, and this is the patient part. A few minutes on most days, with the right fingers, does more than any amount of trying to go faster.
profile.road.childPace.building.4: {speed} for now. Speed is the last thing to arrive and the least worth pushing; accuracy and finger habits come first, and they keep paying back for years afterwards.
profile.road.childPace.building.5: {speed} today, and nothing here needs fixing. Children learn where the keys are long before they build any pace at all, and learning where the keys are is exactly what this practice is for.
profile.road.childPace.building.6: {speed} so far, and regular beats long. Ten minutes a day teaches far more than an hour at the weekend, and it keeps the whole thing something they will come back to.
profile.road.childPace.building.7: {speed} at present. If they are still hunting for letters, that hunting is the work rather than a sign of falling behind — every letter found is one they will not have to look for again.
profile.road.childPace.building.8: {speed} today, and it is worth not timing them. Racing a child at this stage tends to produce quick two-finger typing, which is far harder to unlearn later than slow, correct typing is to speed up.
profile.road.childPace.context.1: For context, {lo}–{hi} words a minute is typical at age {age} — and please don’t measure this against adult speeds, which are quoted everywhere and belong to grown-ups who have typed for years.
profile.road.childPace.context.2: Children of {age} usually land somewhere between {lo} and {hi} words a minute. The figures you will find online are adult ones, and they are not the right yardstick here.
profile.road.childPace.context.3: As a rough guide, {lo}–{hi} words a minute is ordinary at {age}. Adult benchmarks are a different sport altogether.
profile.road.childPace.context.4: Most {age}-year-olds sit around {lo}–{hi} words a minute, and it is worth remembering that very nearly every number quoted online is an adult’s.
profile.road.childPace.context.5: At {age}, anything from {lo} to {hi} words a minute is perfectly ordinary. The adult averages you may have read are twenty years of practice away.
profile.road.childPace.context.6: The usual band at {age} is {lo}–{hi} words a minute — a long way below the adult figures, and rightly so.
profile.road.childPace.context.7: For a child of {age}, {lo}–{hi} words a minute is the normal range. Setting that beside an adult’s speed is comparing two quite different things.
profile.road.childPace.context.8: Typical for {age} is {lo}–{hi} words a minute. That is the number worth holding in mind, rather than the 40 or 60 wpm written for grown-ups.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.1: At {speed} they are right where they should be. What matters at this age is turning up regularly and using the right fingers; speed follows on its own, over years.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.2: {speed} is a healthy pace for this age, and the thing worth protecting now is the habit rather than the number.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.3: {speed} — comfortably in the normal range. Keep the sessions short and regular and this part rather looks after itself.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.4: They are doing well at {speed}. There is little to gain from pushing for more; at this age the progress comes from accuracy, and from each finger doing its own job.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.5: Right on track at {speed}. Children’s typing climbs in steps over years, with long flat stretches in between — and the flat stretches are normal, not a sign that something has stalled.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.6: {speed} says the habit is working. Doing much the same again tomorrow is the whole strategy from here.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.7: No concerns at {speed}. The most useful thing you can do now is keep it enjoyable — a child who likes practising will out-type one who is made to.
profile.road.childPace.onTrack.8: {speed} is good going. If you would like to help, watch which fingers they use rather than the clock; that is what decides where they end up.
profile.road.childPace.starting.1: Nothing on this profile yet. The first few sessions are the ones where a keyboard stops being a puzzle, and they are slow going for everybody.
profile.road.childPace.starting.2: No practice recorded here so far. When they begin, expect it to feel slow for a while — that slowness is the learning, not a problem with it.
profile.road.childPace.starting.3: This page fills in once they start. Short, regular sessions are what make it move; length matters far less than coming back.
profile.road.childPace.starting.4: The charts wake up after the first session. A few minutes at a time is plenty to begin with, and more than enough to build the habit.
profile.road.childPace.starting.5: Nothing to show just yet. The thing to watch for early on is which fingers they use — that decides far more than how quickly they get going.
profile.road.childPace.starting.6: No lessons on this profile yet. Whenever they start is soon enough; there is no age at which this gets harder to pick up.

report.sheet.howToRead.body: Words per minute counts a word as five characters including spaces, which is the standard convention, so it can be compared with figures from anywhere else. Typical is the median of lessons in the period rather than the average, so one exceptional lesson does not move it. Accuracy counts a keystroke as correct only the first time: a corrected mistake still counts as a mistake, because the aim is to stop making it rather than to fix it quickly.

terms.account.1: Accounts are for humans — no bots or automated sign-ups, please.
terms.account.2: One account per household, with a learner profile for each person in it. You do not need an account each.
terms.account.3: Accounts are for adults. If you add a profile for a child, you are telling us you are their parent or guardian and that you consent on their behalf — and the profile, its practice and its deletion are yours to control.
terms.account.4: You are responsible for keeping your sign-in secure, whichever way you use. If someone gets into your account because your password or your provider leaked, we cannot undo what they did. Your account page lists recent sign-ins so you can spot one you did not make, and a passkey or two-step verification makes that far less likely in the first place.
terms.account.p: You don’t need an account at all: as a guest, everything works and your progress lives in your own browser. If you choose to sign in so your progress can follow you across devices, a few simple rules apply:
terms.cert.p1: A certificate says that a named learner typed at a measured speed and accuracy, in a particular language, on a particular date. It is issued by us and it is not a qualification recognised by anybody else — no examination board, no school system, no employer has agreed to accept it. It is honest evidence of what somebody did here, and it is worth exactly that.
terms.cert.p2: To earn one, the practice has to satisfy every condition on the Course page and then the learner has to pass a short assessment. Both are judged on our servers, not in your browser, so the criteria cannot be edited from the outside.
terms.cert.p3: Every certificate carries a number that anybody can check on our Check a certificate page. You choose whether the holder’s name is shown to whoever checks it. We will withdraw a certificate if we find it was obtained by cheating, and you can ask us to withdraw one of yours at any time.
terms.change.p: If we update these terms, the new version appears on this page with a fresh date at the top. Meaningful changes will be visible — no silent rewrites. Continuing to use KeyLearn after a change means you accept the updated terms.
terms.content.p1: Every keystroke statistic, lesson result, and streak you generate belongs to you — and to each learner in your household, whose profile can be exported or deleted on its own. You can download a full copy from your account at any time, and you can erase everything, locally or from our servers. We claim no ownership over your practice data, ever.
terms.content.p2: Where you write something we can see — a support message, a public profile name, a theme you choose to share — you keep it, and you give us only what we need to show it back to you and to run the service.
terms.fair.p1: Use KeyLearn the way it’s meant to be used: to learn typing. Don’t attack, overload, or attempt to break the service, don’t try to access other people’s data, and don’t use the site for anything that’s illegal where you live. Accounts that break these rules may be suspended or removed.
terms.fair.p2: The leaderboards and the multiplayer races are meant to be typed. A result produced by a script, a macro or a second person is not a result, and we will remove it and the account behind it.
terms.glance.1: KeyLearn is open source, and learning to type is free — every lesson, every learner, no ads. Supporting the project is voluntary and unlocks nothing.
terms.glance.2: Be a human, keep one account per person, and don’t use KeyLearn to do anything illegal or harmful.
terms.glance.3: Your typing data is yours — you can export it or erase it whenever you like, for the whole household or one learner at a time.
terms.glance.4: Certificates are ours to issue and real to check, but they are not a qualification anybody else has agreed to recognise.
terms.glance.5: We run this service with care but without warranties: it’s provided as-is, and features may change.
terms.pay.p1: Everything KeyLearn offers is free. Where you choose to support the project voluntarily, payment is handled by our payment provider — we never see or store your card details. Amounts are shown before you confirm, including any tax that applies where you live.
terms.pay.p2: Voluntary contributions are gifts rather than purchases: they unlock nothing, and they are not refundable. If that ever changes — if we introduce something paid — we will say so plainly here first.
terms.title: Terms of Service
terms.warranty.p: We work hard to keep KeyLearn fast, correct, and available, but it is provided as is, without warranties of any kind. Features may change, be added, or retire as the app evolves. We are not liable for damages arising from your use of the service — the most reliable safety net for your progress is the one-click export in your profile. Some jurisdictions don’t allow certain liability limits, so parts of this section may not apply to you.
terms.what.p: KeyLearn is an open-source touch-typing tutor. The entire source code is published under the GNU AGPL license, and you’re welcome to read it, run your own copy, or improve it. Learning to type is free: every lesson and every learner in your household, with no advertising. You can support the project voluntarily, and where you pay us anything the payment terms below apply. Using the site means you accept the terms on this page; if you ever disagree with them, simply stop using the service.
